CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay at the table and work toward a framework that trades large, time-bound U.S. purchase packages (agriculture, energy) and targeted IP/market-access language for a continued freeze of the List 3 hike and a path to rolling back existing Section 301 duties. Do not reopen tariff or hostage escalation, and do not accept a unilateral U.S. snap-back enforcement regime or deep SOE/industrial-policy rewrite as the price of a March summit. Keep Meng/Huawei on a separate legal track while using talks to reduce the chance the United States converts the criminal case into a broader tech blockade.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is material but not existential. Combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is already about $250B of Chinese exports (25% on the $50B Lists 1–2; 10% on List 3), and firm-level targeting is live: the April 2018 ZTE denial order, the 1 Dec 2018 Meng arrest, and the 28 Jan 2019 Huawei/Meng indictments. China’s export engine is already weakening—December 2018 exports fell 4.4% and imports 7.6%, PMI slipped below 50, and official growth talk has shifted to a 6–6.5% 2019 target—while U.S. customs imports from China dropped from $52.1B (Oct 2018) to $31.1B (Mar 2019), about −40%. That maps near the CHN +0.5 anchor (export hit + Huawei targeting) but below it because the most dangerous near-term shock—the scheduled List 3 jump from 10% to 25%—was suspended at the G20 and then delayed again on 24 Feb after Trump cited “substantial progress,” and the original 1 Mar deadline passed without a hike. Action should be mild and deal-seeking, not escalatory: a new tariff or detention move would likely collapse the Washington/Beijing rounds just as Trump is advertising a possible Mar-a-Lago close and as U.S. farm-belt purchases (extra soybeans; talk of ~$30B/year of ag) are the one area where China can move without rewriting the development model. Full concession or formal purchase lock-in is premature: U.S. existing tariffs remain, enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer/SOE issues are still unresolved, and domestic room for “bowing” is limited. Negotiate—use purchases and limited legal/IP language as bargaining chips, hold the line on snap-back and core industrial policy, and convert the tariff delay into a durable freeze.
key_factors: Section 301 still covers ~$250B of Chinese exports; List 3 remains at 10% after the Feb 24 delay
Huawei/Meng criminal-extradition track plus prior ZTE denial order is a live tech/sovereignty threat
China real-economy stress: Dec 2018 export/import contraction, PMI <50, lower 2019 growth target
U.S. imports from China down ~40% Oct 2018–Mar 2019, confirming demand destruction in the bilateral channel
Talks advanced on purchases/currency MOUs but still gapped on structural reform and enforcement
Trump is signaling deal-seeking (hike delay, possible Mar-a-Lago summit), which raises the payoff to staying in talks versus escalating

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
G20 Buenos Aires dinner: 90-day negotiation window; planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
US DOJ unseals fraud and sanctions-related charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests Meng's extradition from Canada.
Trump tweets that talks have made substantial progress and further delays the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25%.
The original 90-day tariff-hike deadline passes without an increase (already delayed on Feb 24).
U.S. imports of goods from China fell from $52.08B (2018-10) to $31.08B (2019-03), a −40.3% decline over the window.
China's December exports unexpectedly fell 4.4% and imports 7.6%; analysts said Beijing may be more eager to strike a trade deal and will need more aggressive measures to stabilize GDP growth.
Trump delayed the List 3 increase citing progress on IP, tech transfer, agriculture and other issues, but no signed agreement or enforcement mechanism; hoped to conclude with Xi at Mar-a-Lago.
Significant gap remains on structural and tech-transfer issues; China has not offered an acceptable enforcement mechanism; fundamental SOE/model changes remain a nonstarter in Beijing.
